hero.title: Government of India Act, 1935
hero.description: Master the Government of India Act, 1935—the monumental legislation that shaped modern India's federal structure, introduced Provincial Autonomy, established the Federal Court, and served as the primary administrative blueprint for the Constitution of India (UPSC GS Paper-II).

timeline.title: Road to the 1935 Act
timeline.description: Key historical events and constitutional developments that culminated in the Government of India Act, 1935.

cards.details: A statutory commission appointed to look into the functioning of the constitutional system in India, recommending the abolition of diarchy and the establishment of a federation.
Prepared by a committee headed by Motilal Nehru, outlining a draft constitution for India demanding Dominion status and a federal structure.
Three conferences held in London to discuss constitutional reforms in India based on the Simon Commission report, involving Indian political leaders and British representatives.
Published by the British Government containing proposals for constitutional changes, which were later examined by a Joint Select Committee of the British Parliament.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Retain key provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935 using simple memory hooks.

items.title: Mnemonic 1
items.decryption: Federal Court established (1937), Autonomy in provinces introduced, Communal electorates extended (to depressed classes, women, and labor), Three-fold division of legislative powers (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent), Safeguards and special responsibilities vested in the Governor-General.

items.title: Mnemonic 2
items.decryption: Remember that the Reserve Bank of India was created to control currency and credit, and the franchise (voting rights) was extended to about 10% of the total population.

items.title: Mnemonic 3
items.decryption: Division of powers: Federal (59), Provincial (54), Concurrent (36). Governor-General retains residuary powers.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Test your instant recall of facts related to the 1935 Act before taking the tests.

items.question: Did the proposed All-India Federation under the 1935 Act ever come into existence?
items.answer: No. The federation never materialized because the princely states refused to join it.

items.question: How were legislative subjects divided under the Government of India Act, 1935?
items.answer: Into three lists: Federal List (59 items), Provincial List (54 items), and Concurrent List (36 items).

items.question: In whom were the residuary legislative powers vested under the 1935 Act?
items.answer: The residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General of India.

items.question: Which institution established in 1937 was the predecessor of the Supreme Court of India?
items.answer: The Federal Court of India, established in Delhi.

items.question: How did the 1935 Act change the system of Diarchy?
items.answer: It abolished diarchy in the provinces and introduced it at the Centre (though the central diarchy provisions were never fully implemented).

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Assuming that the Federal Court of India established in 1937 was the final court of appeal. In reality, it was not. Appeals from the Federal Court could still be carried to the Privy Council in London.

Trap 2: Believing that residuary legislative powers were given to either the Federal or Provincial Legislatures. Under the 1935 Act, residuary powers were uniquely vested in the Governor-General of India to decide which list a new subject belonged to.
Trap 3: Confusing the abolishment of diarchy. Remember: Diarchy was abolished in the provinces and introduced at the Centre. Do not mix up the two levels of government.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Comprehensive structured analysis of the Government of India Act of 1935 for UPSC Prelims and Mains.

sections.title: 1. All-India Federation & Division of Powers (with Diarchy at Centre)
sections.content:
Proposed Federal Structure

The Act provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of British Indian Provinces and Princely States as units. The federation, however, never came into existence as the required number of princely states did not sign the Instrument of Accession.

List NameNumber of ItemsKey Representative SubjectsJurisdiction
Federal List59External Affairs, Defence, Currency & Coinage, Census, Posts & TelegraphsFederal Legislature
Provincial List54Police, Provincial Public Services, Education, Land Revenue, Public HealthProvincial Legislature
Concurrent List36Civil Procedure, Criminal Law, Marriage & Divorce, Civil & Labor RelationsBoth Federal & Provincial

Diarchy at the Centre

The Act abolished diarchy in the provinces and replaced it with Diarchy at the Centre. Federal subjects were divided into:

  • Reserved Subjects: Administered by the Governor-General with the help of counsellors appointed by him (e.g., Defence, External Affairs, Ecclesiastical affairs). Not answerable to the legislature.
  • Transferred Subjects: Administered by the Governor-General on the advice of ministers responsible to the legislature (not exceeding 10).

sections.title: 2. Provincial Autonomy, Bicameralism & Provincial Executive
sections.content:
Provincial Autonomy

The Act abolished diarchy in provinces and introduced Provincial Autonomy. The provinces were allowed to act as autonomous units of administration in their defined spheres. Governors were required to act on the advice of ministers responsible to the provincial legislatures. This came into effect in 1937 and was suspended in 1939 due to WWII outbreaks.

Provincial Bicameralism

It introduced bicameralism in 6 out of 11 provinces. These legislative chambers consisted of a Legislative Council (Upper House) and a Legislative Assembly (Lower House), although many limitations and safeguards were placed on them:

  • Bicameral Provinces (6): Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, and the United Provinces.
  • Unicameral Provinces (5): Punjab, Central Provinces, Sindh, Orissa, and North-West Frontier Province (NWFP).

sections.title: 3. Federal Court, Reserve Bank of India, and Institutional Safeguards
sections.content:
Institutional Establishments

The Act recommended the creation of several key national institutions to consolidate the federal nature of administration, finance, and services across British India.

Other Crucial Administrative Provisions:

  • Extension of Franchise: Extended the franchise (right to vote) to approximately 10% of the total population, giving political voice to millions of new voters.
  • Communal Representation: It extended the principle of communal representation by providing separate electorates for depressed classes (scheduled castes), women, and labor (workers).
  • Abolition of Indian Council: It abolished the Council of India established by the Government of India Act 1858. The Secretary of State for India was instead provided with a team of advisers.
  • Reorganization of Provinces: Burma was completely separated from India under the provisions of this Act. Two new provinces, Orissa and Sind, were also created.
